This is not a new argument.

To quote an ancient Roman saying, "de gustibus non est disputandum."

Our taste in cinema is subjective (because it is the result of the bilateral relationship between \[us and cinema\] within a specific cultural, personal, and historical context), but it necessarily corresponds to objective historicity (the history of cinema in a determined place within its intellectual, technical, and technological development \[not necessarily *evolution*\]; namely, cinema today is not the same as cinema in 1910, for better *and* for worse \[for diverse reasons\]).

In other words, it's valid for you not to like a movie (because various cinematic schools, philosophies, genres, techniques, etc., come into play, as well as personal psychological complexities, such as not liking violence, for instance). 

But claiming that The Killer is the worst film ever made, from the perspective of the study of art is objectively false. This is because The Killer is the result of a specific cinematic development (I insist: cultural, intellectual, technical), and objectively, The Killer is better than any primitive film where the language of cinema was just being gradually discovered.

Ironically saying it as hyperbole to make a point (namely, that you hated The Killer) is valid, I guess. Although, personally, I don't understand it.

By the way, this pseudo-analysis that I'm attempting (poorly) is also the result of a specific point in (my) history lol.

Idk, what do you guys think?

Film Taste is subjective, but the medium is also the go-to for monumental auteurs and visionaries. What I mean to say is that there is an objectivity to The Great films and being able to say that they are doing something very unique/idiosyncratic/remarkable/affecting, and that the project has something distinct to it regardless of personally liking or disliking it. 

There is a certain objectivity to being able to recognize art for art and not entertainment regardless if you personally like or dislike it, agree or disagree with it, because the alternative is populism.

Yes absolutely there is objectivity in cinema, because cinema is like a language, with its own rules, syntax and grammar.

For example, if a filmmaker shows us the exterior of a building, and then cuts to a character in an interior space, that is inherently implying that the interior space is inside that building we've just seen, even if in real life the interior is an artificially set thousands of miles from the building. But because over a century of film has created the language of the "establishing shot", and because we as audiences have learned the language of cinema through watching and absorbing them, it is understandable to us.

So on a fundamental level, yes filmmaking can be objectively good or bad, because a film that completely ignores the rules of the language will end up being confusing and inexplicable to audiences.

Then there are basic technical considerations, like are the shots in focus, the dialogue audible, the music appropriate for the scene? Again, they might seem trivial, but watch a film that screws up these things and you'll see there very much is something that is objectively bad.

But I would argue that the objectivity extends to more complex considerations like character, theme and plot. For example, have you ever seen a film where you completely misunderstood an important plot detail? Or felt like the resolution was completely unearned or false? On a much more intricate level, these films are missing something vital in the storytelling "rules" by perhaps omitting important information or misleading the audience unintentionally.

There is indeed a grey area where audience interpretation and taste enters the equation, but again, I would say that sometimes the flaws in a film are down to the actual mechanics of script/direction/editing rather than the viewer just not "getting" it.

Of course, rules are meant to be broken, and like any language, the language of cinema is changing and evolving, and it's filmmakers who experiment with the form, break the rules and introduce new concepts that push the medium forward.

No.

Screenwriters, producers, directors, editors, and film studios can have personal agendas, some of which go in conflict with other individuals in the filmmaking process.

The reverse is true for viewing - every human has some sort of societal or aesthetic bias, so the concept of objective evaluation is mythical.

It's not a correct understanding of the term, but I've always thought Keats' "negative capability" is as close as a critic/viewer can get to objectivity. The actual term refers to a writer's ability to create truth and perfection that's obviously impossible. To "understand the unknown."

My bastardization of this concept for criticism is like enhanced empathy, where you can watch an otherwise shitty movie (or just one you dislike) and understand why people enjoy it. This is what I came to while trying to figure out why the fuck my aunt loves Jack and Jill.

There is the idea that “I don’t know art but I know what I like.” My problem is that most people like this are the loudest people on the room. I went to school for sound design in film and I promise you no one at Thanksgiving gave a fuck what u thought about any film being brought up. Took me a while to accept that a lot of people see those with actual knowledge as a threat to their opinion and go on the “head in the sand” attack or the “that is the worst movie ever” attack. In regards to your point. I love it. I agree with its question and how valid it is and my answer is it depends.  Do you care about someone’s opinion? If so then maybe take it for that.  Or do you know they know more? Like how the lighting or costume design hit just right and that overshadowed a badly written third act. I find that movies falling apart aren’t near as big of a deal to me if they were fun to watch.  Most people on the other hand seem to boil a movies worth down to its ending. I don’t know why. Except in Enemy. That ending ruined the movie for me because I read it was not suppose to make sense. Which my wife loved the idea of. I love her so it gave me pause. I watched it again and its nonsensical nature makes it feel like what’s the point? Now I’m rambling. I hope some of this is pertinent and thanks for the back and forth.
